match.reason: The closest bank point, e-scarcity, covers the same unlimited-wants-versus-scarce-resources core but is broader, adding factors of production, opportunity cost and renewable resources, and it never frames the what, how and for whom decisions the new point needs, so it would teach more than this point.

draft.title: The basic economic problem
card: Wants are unlimited. People always want more goods and services than they have. Resources are limited, so they are scarce.
Scarcity is the gap between unlimited wants and limited resources. Every society faces it, rich or poor, so choices must be made.
Scarcity forces three questions. What and how much should be made? How should it be made? Who gets what is made?
The how question is about methods, such as using more workers or more machines. The who question is about how output is shared among people.
draft.remember: Unlimited wants meet limited resources, so every society must answer what, how and who.

a.q: Why does every society face the basic economic problem?
opts: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
Resources are unlimited but wants are limited
Poor societies have too few goods to share
Governments choose to make some goods rare
a.why: Scarcity comes from unlimited wants meeting limited resources. It is not only a problem of poor societies, because rich societies still cannot meet every want.
a.clue: Think about the gap between wants and resources.

b.q: The Victorian town of Marlow has one new hospital site. Its council debates whether to build a hospital or a sports centre. Which question is the council answering?
opts: What to make, given limited resources
How to make it, given limited resources
Who gets it, given limited resources
How to remove scarcity in the town
b.why: The council is choosing which good to make, so it is answering the what question. It is not choosing a method of production or who receives the output, and choosing between two uses does not remove scarcity.
b.clue: Is the council choosing a good, a method or a group of people?

a.best: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited

b.best: What to make, given limited resources

problems.detail: The stem says the town has 'one new hospital site' and then says the council is choosing between a hospital and a sports centre. Calling it a hospital site suggests the choice is already made, which is confusing. 'One vacant site' or 'one block of land' would be clearer.

In Victoria, public hospitals are planned and funded by the state government, not by local councils, so a council choosing whether to build a hospital is unrealistic. A council choosing between a library and a sports centre, or the state government choosing between a hospital and a sports centre, would be accurate.
